blocks.text: There are, however, interpreters who take the word שחר in the sense of darkness, with which the dense swarms of locusts obscure the sun. So Abu-Walid, cited by Pococke p. 116: שבה אנתשאר אלגראר פי אלבלאד באנתשאר אלצו פי אלגו הדא קול גירנא וחשביהם באנתשאר אלטלאם אולא, the spreading of the locusts over the region is compared to the spreading of light in the air. This is what others say. But the comparison with the spreading of darkness is more fitting, as is said in Exod. X, 15: They covered the face of the whole earth, so that the earth was [III, 306] darkened. But R. Tanchum, Pococke adds, who no doubt had seen him and weighed his opinion, thinks otherwise. For after saying that he compares אנתשאר אלגראד באנתשאר אלצו אנר אלצבאה, the spreading of the locusts with the spreading of the light of the dawn, he adds: וקיל אן שחר הנא אלטלאם משתק מן שחור אי אנה יחגב אלצו לכתרתה פיציר אלטלאם מבסוטא עלי אלגבאל כמא קאל, and it is said (by some) that שחר here is darkness, derived from שחור, to be black, because by their multitude they block or veil the light, so that darkness is thereby spread over the mountains, according to what he said before, a day of darkness and gloom, which agrees with what we find in Exod. X, 15: They covered the surface of the whole earth. But he says: אלאול אטהר ואנסב, the former opinion is clearer and more fitting. — C. G. Justi, in his notes on this passage, holds that the noun שחר is to be taken in the sense of twilight, because the notion of something joyful is attached to the dawn, which in no way suits this passage. — Francisco Alvarez writes in his Accounts of Journeys Made through Ethiopia that swarms of locusts shine in the sky with the yellow colour of their wings, and that from this shining the Ethiopians recognize their approach before they arrive; and it is Oedmann's opinion, in den Vermischten Sammlungen, fasc. 6, ch. 8, p. 75, that the words of Joel allude to the same thing.

Oedmann, fasc. 6, ch. 8, p. 77, relates the words behind them a flame will burn to the fact that places laid waste by locusts truly look as if scorched by fire, as Mariti reports in his Account of a Journey Made through the Island of Cyprus, vol. 1, p. 258, since locusts consume not only crops and grasses but also the roots.

The locusts passing over our heads roared with the sound of a great cataract, says Forsskål in Descript. Animall. p. 81. A learned Maronite affirmed the very same to Norberg; his account may be read in Norberg's ninth letter in vol. 6, part 2 of Björnståhl's collection of letters (Biörnstähls Briefe auf seinen ausländischen Reisen, Sechsten Bandes Zweytes Heft), pp. 364–365.

The Alexandrinus: καὶ ἐν τοις βελεσιν αὐτοι πεσενται, καὶ ου μη συντελεσθωσι [kai en tois belesin autoi pesentai, kai ou mē syntelesthōsi]. The Vulgate translator: and they will fall through the windows, and will not be destroyed. The Syriac: ܛܠ ܡܣܘܢܝܗܘܢ ܢܦܠܘܢ ܘܠܐ ܢܫܠܡܘܢ ܨܒܘ ܠܥܝܢܐ, they will fall under the weight of their arms, and will not bring the matter to an end. The Chaldee: גבר בכבישיה אזלין לאתר דאנין שליחין קטלין ולא מקבלין ממון, each goes along his path to the place to which they are sent; they slaughter, and do not accept money. “It is evident,” says Pococke p. 144, “that the root בצע has various meanings. 1. It denotes to make gain, or to be greedy for profit or gain, as in Proverb. XV, 27, בוצע בצע, one who is given to gain, and Habac. II, 9, בוצע בצע רע, greedy of evil gain, and often elsewhere; and in this sense the Chaldee uses it here. An Arabic manuscript translated it from the Hebrew thus: ورا السلاح يقعون ولا يطمعون [wa-rā al-silāḥ yaqaʿūna wa-lā yaṭmaʿūna], they will fall behind the sword, and will not make gain. 2. To complete, or to bring to an end, as in Esaj. X, 12, כי יבצע יהוה את כל מעשהו, when the Lord has completed all his work, and Lament. II, 17, בצע אמרתו, he has fulfilled his word. In this sense the Greek, the printed Arabic [in the Polyglots], and the Syriac took it. 3. To cut down, cut off, wound, as in Iob. VI, 9, ויבצעני, and that he would cut me down, and Esaj. XXXVIII, 12, ויבצעני, he will cut me off, and Amos. IX, 1, ובצעם, and strike them (or wound them, as in the margin); and thus it agrees with פצע (ב and פ being interchanged), which de- [III, 314] notes to wound. This meaning R. Tanchum also confirms from the Arabic language, in which بضع [baḍaʿa] means to cut up, to split, or to break into pieces, as also in Chaldee. Therefore both in him and in Abu Walid we read here لا ينجرحون [lā yanjariḥūna], they will not be wounded.”

That certain ancient copies once had Βρωμον [Brōmon] is clear also from the Arabic version in the Polyglots, which was translated from the Alexandrian Greek, since it has: ويصعد نتنه وترتفع رايحته [wa-yaṣʿadu natnuhu wa-tartafiʿu rāyiḥatuhu], and its stench will go up, and its smell will rise.
